hookLine: Spain expels its Jews, and ships reach the Americas; both shaped centuries of suffering

lines: A DECREE: LEAVE, AND NEVER RETURN.
cards: Two documents from one year. The first is a royal decree, signed by Ferdinand and Isabella, the king and queen of Spain. It orders every Jew in their kingdoms to leave by a fixed deadline and never return.
Only baptism would let a family stay. The second is the opening of a sailor's journal.
Christopher Columbus writes to those same two monarchs, and in one stretch of thought he mentions the Jews being driven out, and his own orders to sail west. Same rulers. Same year.

teach.h: A DECREE, AND FAMILIES ON THE ROAD.
teach.b: Start with the decree. Jewish families had lived in Spain for generations: doctors, weavers, translators, neighbors. Now they had until the deadline to choose.
Some were baptized and stayed, and they and their children often lived under suspicion from the Inquisition.

Others sold what they could, left homes and graves behind, and went to Portugal, North Africa, the lands of the Ottoman sultan. Their descendants, called Sephardic Jews, carried the language and songs of Spain with them.
Next, the journal. Columbus reaches an island in the Caribbean, and the Taíno come out to meet the ships.
He writes that they are gentle, that they carry no weapons, and almost in the same breath that they would make good servants. That sentence turned out to be a forecast.
What followed for the peoples of the islands and the mainland was forced labor, war and disease, and whole communities were lost. Then, the hard part for Catholics.

teach.h: BOTH TOLD IN THE LANGUAGE OF FAITH.
teach.b: Both stories were told in the language of faith: the decree spoke of protecting it, the voyage of carrying it.

Catholic teaching today says plainly that faith must never be forced, and recent popes have asked forgiveness for wrongs done by the Church's members. Remembering honestly is not the same as hating the past.
It means letting both documents stand, without cutting either.
Psalm one hundred twenty-nine begins, "Out of the depths I have cried to thee, O Lord: Lord, hear my voice." It is a prayer that fits exiles, and people whose land was taken, too.

how: Catholic memory of these wrongs is public as well as personal: John Paul II's Day of Pardon in the Jubilee year 2000 confessed sins against the people of Israel and against the rights of peoples, and Pope Francis has asked forgiveness for crimes against the native peoples of the Americas during the conquest.

games.q: you're a Jewish weaver in Spain. the decree is read in the square: leave by the deadline and never return. only baptism lets you stay. what do the families around you do?
o: some are baptized and stay; others sell what they can and go.
the decree is withdrawn before the deadline.
games.why: both happened. some were baptized and stayed, often under suspicion; others left homes and graves behind for Portugal, North Africa and the Ottoman lands.

practice: Bring to mind the Jewish families who walked out of Spain, and the families today who come from them, and stay there a few breaths.
Then bring to mind the Taíno and the peoples of the Americas, and those living today who come from them.
If you pray, pray for both with the psalm's words, out of the depths; if you don't, simply hold the two groups of people in your attention, one after the other, without hurrying.

wordCard.voice: Sephardic. The name for the Jews exiled from Spain in 1492, who carried its language and songs into exile. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: remember honestly. Both documents stay on the page, together. Day eight hundred thirty-seven.
